SynCLIP: Synonym-Coherent Language-Image: CLIP-based detectors and segmenters fail when the language shifts—'coffee mug' and 'ceramic mug' should point to the same object, but produce completely different spatial attention maps. Semantic-consistent spatial attention alignment explicitly synchronizes the attention patterns across synonyms during pretraining, so the visual features respond consistently to any words that mean the same thing. This prevents inconsistency in dense predictions across linguistic variation.
Looking Beyond the Window: Global-Local: High-resolution segmentation with CLIP requires sliding-window inference, but processing each window independently breaks semantic continuity—objects at window boundaries get mislabeled because each window sees only its local context. Global-local attention normalization dynamically rescales attention across windows using globally representative proxy queries, so a pixel near the edge sees its full semantic context, not just what fits in one window. The result: consistent pixel labels across the entire image, not a patchwork.
Do Visual-Language Grid Maps Capture Lat: A robot builds a semantic map by embedding images with CLIP and storing the features at each location—but does this map actually generalize to new scenes and queries? Without a rigorous evaluation methodology, teams deploy maps blind to their actual semantic quality. This paper defines semantic coverage metrics and transfer benchmarks that measure whether the embedding space truly captures object identity across viewpoints and instances.
Learning Generalizable Feature Fields fo: Mobile manipulation needs a single scene representation that handles both fine-grained geometry (where exactly do I grasp?) and large-scale spatial structure (how do I navigate there?). Unified feature fields that couple visual embeddings with geometric detail let the robot query the space by language for both high-level navigation targets and low-level grasp affordances, replacing the traditional separation between semantic maps and geometric models.
SRA-Det: Omni-Grained Open-Vocabulary De: Open-vocabulary detectors score boxes against category embeddings, but real queries are richer: 'red mug' is not just 'mug'—it combines identity and color, and simple text embedding misses that faceted structure. Semantic Retrieval Augmentation with learnable semantic facets decomposes queries into multiple fine-grained attributes and reasons over them jointly, scoring boxes by soft-min matching that weighs all facets. The detector now sees 'red' as a separate semantic signal, not noise mixed into the 'mug' embedding.
PET-DINO: Unifying Visual Cues into Grou: Grounding DINO detects and grounds objects using visual prompts (a reference image or box), but prompt diversity—different image angles, lighting, backgrounds—hurts generalization. Training-time visual prompt augmentation is expensive and often suboptimal. Prompt-enriched training with dynamic memory distillation learns to transform diverse visual prompts into stable features that align with text embeddings, so the detector generalizes across prompt variations without manual augmentation.
ViTPrompt: Training-Free Prompt Refineme: Test-time refinement for open-vocabulary detection usually improves classification confidence but leaves bounding boxes noisy, since boxes and classes are optimized separately. Inserting visual tokens from high-confidence detections directly into the text prompt adds instance-aware geometric context without any retraining. Visual token augmentation lets the prompt encoder see the spatial structure the detector already found, refining both box coordinates and scores in a single pass.
Detect Everything with Few Examples: Open-world robot manipulation needs to detect object categories with only a handful of demonstrations, no fine-tuning, and low latency on the robot. Using ViT features extracted from few exemplars and prototype-based matching, the system learns an open-set detector on the fly. Few-shot prototypical detection with frozen ViT backbones trades off-line training time for real-time adaptation: exemplars seed prototypes, new images are scored by similarity to those prototypes, and the model generalizes across viewpoints and instances without touching the weights.
Mitigating Objectness Bias for Open-Voca: Open-vocabulary panoptic segmentation merges semantic and instance masks, but objectness heads trained on seen classes suppress masks of unseen objects by default—they're never seen as 'objects.' CLIP's text score tells you the semantic signal is there, but the objectness gate kills it. CLIP-conditioned objectness recalibration overrides the objectness head using CLIP scores as a gate signal: if CLIP is confident, the region is treated as foreground even if objectness disagrees.
PCA-Seg: Revisiting Cost Aggregation for: Vision transformers compute cost aggregation—matching features between regions—but aggregation that works for closed-vocabulary segmentation often fails at fine-grained segmentation and unseen classes because it assumes known object geometry. Cost aggregation revisited for open-vocabulary dense prediction decouples feature matching from class-specific spatial priors, letting the model find object boundaries using pure feature consistency. Better aggregation works equally well for parts (within-object structure) and unseen categories, unifying the problem.
Reconstructing CLIP for Open-Vocabulary: CLIP is trained on image-level classification, so its features are global and coarse—a 14×14 grid of patches. Dense prediction needs fine spatial detail that CLIP's pretraining didn't directly optimize. Multi-scale feature reconstruction with spatial pyramid pooling augments CLIP with dense intermediate representations and learnable spatial queries, recovering fine detail at multiple scales. The reconstructed model keeps CLIP's vocabulary while gaining the spatial precision dense tasks demand.
Rethinking MLLM Itself as a Segmenter wi: Multimodal LLMs have vision and language understanding built in, but segmentation typically requires bolting on specialist mask decoders on top, adding complexity, weight, and latency. What if you just extracted high-resolution visual features directly from the MLLM without a separate decoder? Direct high-resolution feature extraction from MLLM internals yields dense spatial features that can be projected to masks with a simple linear layer, making segmentation cheaper and keeping the MLLM frozen.
PEARL: Geometry Aligns Semantics for Tra: Training-free segmentation with frozen VLMs relies on matching image features to text embeddings, but the VLM's global bias—it's trained for classification—fights the per-pixel precision you need. Procrustes alignment rotates the feature space to maximize separability between the target class and background, then Laplacian propagation smooths the resulting confidence map using spatial structure. No training needed; just geometric rotation and diffusion that push the frozen features toward sharper, more coherent boundaries.
The Power of Prior: Training-Free Segmen: LLaVA understands language and vision but wasn't trained to segment, so feeding its features directly to text matching yields poor masks. Yet LLaVA does have semantic and spatial priors baked into its layers. Extracting features from the right layer and applying frozen cosine matching between dense visual features and text embeddings yields surprisingly strong segmentation without any additional training. The 'prior' is simply the feature quality LLaVA already learned.
Direct Segmentation without Logits Optim: Traditional open-vocabulary segmentation iteratively optimizes logits—a slow, indirect loop. The paper reframes the problem as solving distribution discrepancy analytically: homogeneous regions (same semantics everywhere in the region) should map to the same text embedding, so formulate segmentation as a distribution-matching problem with a closed-form solution. No iteration, no optimization loops—just a direct matrix solve that runs in milliseconds and achieves competitive accuracy.
SPAR: Single-Pass Any-Resolution ViT for: Vision Transformers are pretrained at a fixed resolution, and dense prediction at higher resolutions requires sliding-window inference (slow) or extrapolation (unstable). Teacher-student distillation transfers spatial reasoning from a finely-strided sliding-window teacher to a single-pass student, so the student learns to produce high-resolution segmentation maps in one forward pass without the teacher's computational cost. The student inherits the teacher's spatial sensitivity while running 10-50× faster.
Towards Open-World Grasping with Large V: Language-instructed grasping requires both semantic understanding ('grasp the red mug') and precise spatial-geometric reasoning (contact normals, collision checks). VLMs are strong at semantics but weak at spatial details; geometric models miss the language grounding. VLM referring segmentation combined with contact-aware grasp ranking uses the VLM to ground the referred object, then scores candidate grasp poses by contact point quality and clearance. Two streams—semantic and geometric—fuse into a single action.
VLM-Grounder: A VLM Agent for Zero-Shot: 3D visual grounding (pointing to an object in a point cloud based on language) usually needs 3D training data and 3D-aware architectures. Yet a 2D vision-language model can reason about spatial relations if given multiple views of the scene. Reasoning-chain distillation over multiview 2D VLM outputs projects 3D points to several viewpoints, scores each using the 2D VLM, and aggregates using learned spatial reasoning. Zero-shot 3D grounding reaches competitive accuracy on ScanRefer without 3D labels or 3D-specific training.
DeRVOS: Decoupling Trajectory Generation: Referring video segmentation must track a specific referred object ('the person in the red coat') across occlusions and motion in dynamic scenes. Unified models that jointly handle temporal tracking and multimodal fusion often fail under occlusion. Decoupling into consistent trajectory generation and multimodal understanding uses a pretrained video instance segmentation model to generate candidate trajectories, then multimodal fusion selects which trajectory matches the referring expression. Separation of concerns simplifies the problem.
ThinkGrasp: A Vision-Language System for: Grasping heavily occluded objects in clutter requires reasoning about what's hiding beneath and whether removing obstacles first makes sense—pure visual geometry can't answer 'should I move the thing on top of it first?' A vision-language system that reasons about occlusion relationships and strategic removal jointly considers the visible geometry, the language description of the target, and the spatial graph of what's blocking what. The system plans not just where to grasp, but whether the grasp order matters.
GraspSAM: When Segment Anything Meets Gr: Grasp detection usually fails on unfamiliar objects because training data is limited, and users can't easily direct the system to specific regions. GraspSAM adapts SAM (trained on 1B masks) with lightweight adapters and a modified decoder, accepting point, box, or text prompts to predict grasps for any object without category labels. By reusing SAM's massive prior knowledge, the system generalizes to unseen object types and multiple prompt modalities.
SAM-Rectified Part Detection with Iterat: Parts like handles, wheels, and buttons have different geometric and functional properties that affect how a robot should interact with them, yet SAM segments them as visual regions without understanding their distinct roles. The gap is that part segmentation needs to recognize functional identity, not just visual boundaries. This approach fine-tunes SAM on parts, then iteratively refines part masks by matching pose predictions: it detects a part's orientation and pose from the mask, re-prompts SAM with refined regions, and repeats to converge on part masks that align to actual functional geometry.
MovSAM: Single-Image Moving Object Segme: Detecting moving objects normally requires comparing multiple frames—impossible from a single still image. An MLLM reasons step-by-step about scene context to infer motion cues, generating text prompts that SAM uses to segment likely-moving objects with iterative refinement. Semantic reasoning about object behavior bridges the temporal gap that optical flow cannot cross from one image alone.
Low-Effort Iterative Dataset Generation: Hand-labeling instance masks for unfamiliar objects is expensive and limits training data diversity. Change detection (frame differencing) identifies unfamiliar objects automatically, then SAM auto-labels them without human annotation, bootstrapping datasets for new categories. Iterative refinement over multiple frames converges to accurate masks.
Ov3R: Open-Vocabulary Semantic 3D Recons: 3D scene understanding has always required category-specific labels, making it impossible to recognize objects outside the training vocabulary. CLIP3R fuses 2D CLIP embeddings with camera geometry to build instance-level open-vocabulary reconstruction, attaching language-aligned features to each voxel. A single video and a text prompt suffice to locate and segment any object in 3D without 3D training labels.
CoSMo3D: Promptable 3D Semantic Segmenta: Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation must handle partial views and compositional phrases like 'the handle of the mug. ' An LLM guides construction of a canonical shape space where semantically similar parts align across views, then queries are matched in that stable space. Canonical alignment lets the system reason about part identity and spatial attributes without 3D training data.
OpenVoxel: Training-Free Grouping and Ca: Voxel grids provide a simple 3D representation, but they lack semantic labels and grouping — you have occupied voxels but no understanding of which voxels belong to the same object or what that object is. The challenge is achieving object-level semantic understanding in 3D without training on 3D labels. OpenVoxel groups voxels using unsupervised clustering, then uses a frozen MLLM to caption each cluster by reasoning about its geometry and appearance: it performs clustering on voxel positions and features, then queries an MLLM with the cluster's geometry and color to generate a natural-language description, enabling open-vocabulary queries without training.
OpenVox: Real-Time Instance-Level Open-V: Mobile robots need fast, incremental open-vocabulary 3D maps, but real-time segmentation noise accumulates across frames, corrupting the map. A probabilistic voxel SLAM fuses VLM-grounded instances across frames using per-voxel membership probabilities, smoothing detection errors through time. Instance tracking persists object identity even when individual frames are ambiguous.
GraspSplats: Efficient Manipulation with: Continuous 3D fields (NeRFs) encode language-aligned features but require expensive differentiable rendering to sample grasp poses; discrete voxels waste memory. Distilled CLIP features attach directly to 3D Gaussians, enabling direct grasp point sampling via feature lookup rather than rendering. This explicit geometry avoids neural field inference overhead while capturing scenes in 60 seconds.
LensDFF: Language-Enhanced Sparse Featur: Few-shot dexterous manipulation is computationally expensive when systems must reconstruct full 3D scenes (NeRF) for each new object from limited views. 2D visual features distill directly onto simple point clouds, with text descriptions guiding view-consistent feature fusion for single-view generalization. Avoiding full scene reconstruction cuts computational cost while enabling grasp generalization.
DVEFormer: Efficient Dense Visual Embedd: Real-time open-vocabulary scene understanding requires per-pixel language-aligned features, but VLM inference is slow and desktop-bound. Knowledge distillation from an Alpha-CLIP teacher trains an efficient RGB-D Transformer student to predict dense embeddings at 26–77 FPS, running directly on edge hardware. The compact student inherits CLIP alignment without recomputing expensive VLM features.
ExtrinSplat: Decoupling Geometry and Sem: 3D Gaussian splats were designed for geometry — reconstructing shape and appearance from images. Adding semantic features directly to splats conflates two separate problems: some splats might represent background geometry that has no semantic label, while others represent objects that are semantically important. ExtrinSplat decouples geometry splats (for accurate 3D shape) from semantic features (for language grounding): it maintains the original Gaussian geometry for rendering fidelity, but stores language-aligned features in a separate, task-specific layer, avoiding the contamination of geometry with semantic labels.
UZ3DVG: Unaided Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grou: Grounding a phrase like 'the chair to the left of the desk' in a point cloud requires three capabilities: recognizing objects by open-vocabulary labels, understanding spatial relations (left, right, behind), and reasoning about geometry without 3D training data. The challenge is doing this zero-shot when the language grounding model has never seen 3D coordinates. UZ3DVG distills a reasoning-aware chain-of-thought from an MLLM into a geometry-aware 3D model: it uses an MLLM to generate a reasoning trace (identify candidates, check relations, select), then learns to reproduce that reasoning using 3D geometry features and spatial relations, achieving 3D grounding without 3D labels.
SAQN: Semantic-Based Adaptive Query Netw: 3D referring segmentation must resolve class identity and spatial relations simultaneously, but standard point-cloud networks treat them separately. Class-level semantic queries adapt per-instance to reconcile 'which object?' and 'which spatial role?' in a single pass over the point cloud. Adaptive routing lets the network focus on spatial reasoning necessary for disambiguation.
LangRef3DGS: Language-Guided 3D Referent: Identifying 'the red mug in the cabinet' in a 3D Gaussian-splatted scene requires learning object identities from partial views that arrive incrementally. A Dirichlet process discovers latent object categories and maintains open-vocabulary identity across partial observations, grounding referring expressions without closed-set class labels. Non-parametric Bayesian inference lets the system add new identities as views arrive.
QueryMe: Open-Vocabulary 3D Object Affor: A robot grasping an object must locate not just 'the mug' but 'the handle of the mug'—the interactive part. Multimodal reasoning over 3D evidence grounds affordances described in plain language, connecting task intent to geometric grasp opportunities. Task descriptions provide the semantic signal needed to resolve which part is actionable.
Zoo3D: Zero-Shot 3D Object Detection at: 3D object detection at scene level without training labels requires inferring object boundaries from geometry and appearance cues alone. SAM-generated masks cluster via graph structure to form connected 3D regions, with open-vocabulary classification applied to each cluster without any 3D detection training. Graph clustering enforces spatial coherence.
NoOVD: Novel Category Discovery for Open: Open-vocabulary detection covers known classes but struggles to recognize genuinely new categories at deployment time. Metric learning discovers emerging clusters in feature space and assigns them embeddings compatible with the open-vocabulary model, expanding the detector's vocabulary without retraining. New categories integrate via embedding alignment.
Zero-Shot Semantic Segmentation for Robo: Agricultural robots must recognize crops and distinguish weeds, but new weed species constantly emerge and crop varieties vary by region. The challenge is performing segmentation on unseen plant species and weed types without retraining. This approach models crop and weed classes as hyperspheres in a learned feature space, treating unfamiliar weeds as anomalies distant from known crop spheres: it learns a feature space where known crops form tight clusters (hyperspheres) and new weeds appear as outliers, enabling zero-shot detection of unseen species through anomaly scoring in feature space.
OoDIS: Anomaly Instance Segmentation and: Autonomous vehicles encounter unknown objects at deployment, but benchmarks rarely measure instance-level segmentation and detection jointly. OoDIS extends anomaly segmentation benchmarks with instance-level tasks, standardizing evaluation across semantic and instance anomaly understanding. A unified benchmark reveals gaps between detecting unknowns and pinpointing each precisely.
HOPS: Hierarchical Open-Vocabulary Part: Object recognition stops at the category level — 'mug' — but manipulation requires finding specific parts within it. The challenge is that parts like handles, spouts, or buttons don't have a closed taxonomy; they're defined relationally within each object. HOPS tackles this by using hierarchical attention filtering: it extracts which spatial attention heads in a VLM strongly respond to a queried part description, then propagates those activations across the visual feature grid to form a part mask, all without pixel-level part labels.
PCA-Seg: Cost Aggregation for Semantic &: Dense prediction of both objects and parts requires matching every pixel to semantic embeddings, but naive per-pixel matching is noisy and lacks spatial coherence. The problem is that pixels don't exist in isolation — a part boundary should align with actual visual discontinuities in texture or color. PCA-Seg solves this by aggregating similarity costs over local neighborhoods: rather than scoring each pixel independently against text embeddings, it smooths cost over neighborhoods before thresholding, recovering sharp boundaries aligned to visual edges while maintaining open-vocabulary generality.
SRA-Det: Detection Beyond Category Names: Open-vocabulary detectors today score regions against category embeddings like 'mug' or 'chair', but real instructions often specify attributes ('red mug') or parts ('cup handle'). A single region vector is weak for decomposing these multi-faceted descriptions. SRA-Det breaks this by learning separate semantic facets within a detection backbone: it discovers sub-embeddings for category, color, texture, and parts within each region's features, then matches each facet independently to the query, enabling detection of 'red mug' without training on that exact phrase.
Part-Aware Vision-Language Models for Fi: Vision-language models align images to text at the whole-object level, but to recognize fine-grained distinctions — like different handle styles or mug shapes — they must align parts of the image to parts of the description. Without explicit part-level correspondence, a VLM can miss what makes objects different. This approach adds part alignment inside the VLM training: it grounds text mentions of parts ('the curved handle', 'the flat rim') directly to corresponding image regions during contrastive training, so the model learns part-level correspondences that boost fine-grained recognition.
AffordGrasp: In-Context Affordance Reaso: A robot that knows 'mug' doesn't automatically know where to grasp it — affordances (grasp points, push surfaces) depend on the task, not just the object type. When the task is 'pour', the handle is the grasp point; for 'clean', the body is better. The gap is that no label set can enumerate all task-object affordance pairs. AffordGrasp uses an MLLM to infer affordances from task instructions in context: it queries the model with the task description ('pour the coffee into the cup'), the VLM reasons about which part affords that action, then a part segmenter locates it, bridging from words and intent to actionable pose.
RoboPoint: A VLM for Spatial Affordance: Affordances are spatial — they're keypoints or contact regions where interaction succeeds. Naming objects is different from pinpointing where to act on them, yet most models conflate the two. The challenge is predicting action keypoints (grasp points, push locations, insertion ports) for objects never seen in training. RoboPoint frames affordance prediction as keypoint regression in image coordinates: given an object and a task description, it predicts the pixel coordinates where a robot should act, using VLM reasoning to ground task semantics to 2D action points, zero-shot across new objects.
MOKA: Open-World Manipulation through Ma: Robots must reason about how to manipulate unfamiliar objects in open-world settings, but traditional approaches require category-specific policies or dense affordance labels. The problem is bridging from semantic understanding of an object to deciding where and how to grasp or manipulate it, without closed-form affordance labels. MOKA frames affordance reasoning as VLM question-answering over marked regions: it shows the VLM object regions with spatial markers and asks 'which region should I grasp to accomplish X?', letting the model reason through affordances as natural language rather than predicting coordinate outputs.
SemSegGrasp: Task-Oriented Grasping via: Grasping depends on the task: picking up a coffee cup requires grasping the handle, but if the cup is empty and upright, any region works. Most grasping pipelines ignore the semantic task and predict regions uniformly. The key insight is that semantic understanding of an object's parts and their properties should directly drive grasp point selection. SemSegGrasp combines open-vocabulary part segmentation with grasp pose generation: it segments task-relevant parts ('handle', 'body', 'rim') using open-vocab labels, then fits grasp poses to these semantically meaningful regions, ensuring grasps align with task requirements.
One Map to Find Them All: Real-Time Open: Mobile robots navigating natural language instructions ('fetch the water bottle from the kitchen counter') must build a spatial understanding where any object can be queried by text. Traditional semantic maps are discrete, requiring separate training per object class. Building a map that supports querying by arbitrary text in real time is the challenge. This approach builds a single language-aligned feature map by fusing CLIP embeddings across camera frames into a dense 2D/3D map: every map location stores a CLIP feature, so querying for 'counter' or 'water bottle' becomes a similarity search across the map, enabling multi-object navigation without retraining.
Beyond Bare Queries: Open-Vocabulary Gro: Language queries like 'the cup on the table' involve relationships — 'on' — and multiple objects. Grounding requires reasoning about spatial relations between objects, but open-vocabulary systems often treat each phrase as an isolated lookup. Without structured reasoning about object relationships, ambiguous or compositional phrases fail. This approach grounds queries against a 3D scene graph where nodes are detected objects and edges encode spatial relations: a query is decomposed into objects and relations, then matched to the scene graph, allowing 'the cup on the table' to be resolved by finding 'cup' nodes whose 'on' edge points to a 'table' node.
Tag Map: A Text-Based Map for Spatial Re: Dense semantic maps that store VLM embeddings at every pixel are memory-intensive and slow for LLM reasoning over large spaces. Yet robots need to query maps with natural language ('where is the plant?') for navigation and planning. The bottleneck is efficiency: dense embeddings don't scale to large maps or long-horizon planning. Tag Map stores only discrete text labels (or lightweight text embeddings) at sparse landmark locations: instead of embedding every pixel, it maintains a sparse textual map where each point is tagged with descriptive text, enabling LLMs to reason over thousands of object categories at minimal memory cost.
SAGE: Bridging Semantic and Actionable P: A robot must understand both what a part is called ('the drawer pull') and how to manipulate it ('pull it horizontally'). These are different: semantic labels describe identity, but actionable parts require understanding motion axes and constraints specific to articulated objects. The problem is that open-vocabulary segmentation gives semantic parts, but not the motion information grasping and manipulation need. SAGE maps semantic parts to actionable affordances by learning the relationship between named parts and their degrees of freedom: for each articulated object type, it learns which semantic parts correspond to which manipulation axes, allowing 'the slider knob' to map to a linear pull affordance.
HERO: Hierarchical Embedding-Refinement: Videos extend grounding from space to time: 'when the person picks up the mug' refers to a temporal interval, not a box. But text queries operate at multiple timescales — a moment, a clip, a scene context — and naive per-frame matching misses the hierarchical structure. The challenge is matching a linguistic event to temporal windows of varying length while maintaining cross-modal alignment. HERO constructs hierarchical embeddings at four levels (frame, clip, scene, event) and refines them with cross-modal filtering: it generates candidate temporal windows at multiple timescales, extracts multi-level features for each, then filters by similarity to the query embedding, localizing events across temporal granularities.
LangField4D: Spatio-Temporal Continuous: A dynamic 3D scene with moving objects requires tracking identity through time while maintaining semantic meaning. Static 3D fields store per-point features, but objects move, deform, and leave/enter the scene. Querying a dynamic scene by language ('where is the mug moving?') needs both temporal tracking and semantic alignment. LangField4D uses identity-adaptive Gaussians that group over time: it tracks moving object instances across frames using adaptive grouping, stores language-aligned features on the 4D Gaussian representation, and enables queries like 'track the blue mug' to be answered by finding the spatio-temporal region matching the description.
ST4R-Splat: Spatio-Temporal Referring Se: Referring segmentation in 4D requires finding the exact region a phrase points to across space and time. Standard 4D representations track geometry but not semantics; adding semantic labels per frame is expensive. The challenge is maintaining instance identity, spatial precision, and semantic meaning simultaneously in dynamic scenes. ST4R-Splat extends 4D Gaussian splatting with instance awareness and automatic MLLM captioning: it tracks object instances in the splat representation, then uses an MLLM to generate captions for each instance's motion and appearance, enabling spatial-temporal grounding by matching phrases to captioned instance tracks.
OmniGround: A Spatio-Temporal Grounding: Evaluation of video grounding has been limited by small benchmarks with simple queries. Real-world grounding involves complex spatial relations ('to the left of'), temporal complexity ('after the person leaves'), and compositional phrases. Without a large, diverse benchmark, it's hard to drive progress on hard cases. OmniGround provides an 81-category benchmark for complex spatio-temporal grounding: it includes real-world videos with queries involving multiple objects, spatial relations, temporal constraints, and compositional descriptions, providing a standard to measure generalization to naturalistic language in dynamic scenes.
ReAttnCLIP: Training-Free Open-Vocabular: CLIP was trained on internet photos where objects are centered and large, but remote-sensing images are overhead with tiny objects scattered across large areas. Attention patterns trained on whole-image alignment fail for small-scale detection. The problem is that CLIP's spatial attention is miscalibrated for the distribution shift from internet photos to overhead imagery. ReAttnCLIP dynamically redefinines CLIP's attention patterns for overhead imagery without retraining: it analyzes how attention should be weighted for remote-sensing image statistics, adjusting the model's focus to small objects at scale, preserving open vocabulary while adapting to domain priors.
Exploring the Underwater World Segmentat: Underwater images break CLIP: colors shift due to water absorption, scattering creates haze, and the object distribution (fish, coral, kelp) differs radically from internet photos. Off-the-shelf CLIP features perform poorly underwater. Training a new model requires labeled underwater data, which is scarce. The gap is bridging the domain without labeled data or retraining. This approach combines Earth2Ocean (a physics-based color-correction model) with CLIP and a large underwater dataset to establish a baseline: it corrects underwater color shifts using known water properties, then applies CLIP to the corrected images, learning to handle underwater domain shift through data-driven priors rather than retraining.
Thermal-Det: Language-Guided Cross-Modal: Thermal images contain only heat, no RGB, yet CLIP is trained on RGB images and fails on thermal inputs. You cannot directly apply CLIP embeddings to thermal features. The solution is distillation: train a thermal backbone to mimic RGB CLIP's behavior on aligned RGB-thermal image pairs. The challenge is that CLIP operates on a fundamentally different data modality, so naive distillation may fail. Thermal-Det trains a student thermal backbone to match RGB CLIP embeddings through cross-modal distillation on paired RGB-thermal scenes: it learns a mapping from thermal features to CLIP's RGB space, enabling open-vocabulary detection on thermal images while preserving CLIP's semantic generality.
MM-OVSeg: Multimodal Optical-SAR Fusion: Optical images (RGB, multispectral) and SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) images see different aspects of a scene: optical captures appearance, SAR captures physical structure and penetrates clouds. Fusing them for open-vocabulary segmentation requires finding a shared embedding space where both modalities contribute semantically. The challenge is that optical and SAR have no natural alignment and different physical meanings. MM-OVSeg fuses optical and SAR inputs by learning a joint embedding space where both modalities contribute to a unified semantic representation: it trains encoders for each modality to project into a shared CLIP-like space, then performs open-vocabulary segmentation using the fused embeddings, leveraging both view angles to ground language in multi-modal evidence.
